title: Connecting external APIs
notes: Wrap an external API in a thin function with a clear name, like track_parcel, and define it as a tool.
API keys live in your code's environment, never in the prompt, and every call gets a timeout.
Slow down when the API answers 429, and return only the fields the model needs, not the whole response.

slides.title: Connecting external APIs
slides.sub: Wrapping ParcelPath's tracking API as a tool Scout can call safely
sentences: Most tools that matter in real work talk to someone else's system.
For Scout, the big one is ParcelPath, the carrier that delivers Orbit's parcels.
In this lesson you will wrap its tracking API as a tool, and learn the four habits that keep that safe.

slides.title: Why Scout needs two tools in a row

note.text: The output of one tool became the input of the next, and the model made that connection itself.

sentences: Here is why Scout needs the carrier's API.
Ana asks when her tent will arrive.
Scout calls get order, which returns her tracking number, but not where the parcel is right now.
So Scout calls a second tool, track parcel, with that tracking number, and that tool calls ParcelPath.
Now Scout can tell Ana her tent is in transit and due on Thursday.
Notice that the output of one tool became the input of the next, and the model made that connection itself.

slides.title: Wrapping ParcelPath as track_parcel
slides.lead: A thin Python function around the API. httpx, the web client used here, comes with the anthropic package.

rows.out: Ten seconds at most, never forever
A 404 or 500 raises an error, not data
Only what Scout needs, as text

aside.label: Where the key lives
aside.text: HEADERS is built from os.environ["PARCELPATH_KEY"]. The key never appears in the prompt.

sentences: Wrapping an API means writing a thin Python function around it, which takes exactly what the tool definition promises: a tracking number.
It calls ParcelPath with a timeout of ten seconds, so a slow server cannot freeze Scout.
It checks the status code, so a not found or a server error raises an error instead of passing as data.
Then it reads ParcelPath's full answer, which can run to thousands of lines.
And it returns only the fields the model needs, turned into text, because tool results are text.
The API key comes from an environment variable, read inside your code, and it never goes near the prompt.

slides.title: Four habits for every API tool

spokes.label: Keys in env
spokes.sub: never in the prompt or code

note.text: Each habit prevents a real failure: a leaked key, a frozen agent, a blocked account, a flooded context.

sentences: Every API tool you build needs the same four habits.
Keys stay in your environment, read by your code, and never pasted into code files or prompts.
Every call has a timeout, because one day the other side will hang.
Rate limits are respected: when the API answers four twenty-nine, too many requests, you slow down.
And results are trimmed to the fields the model needs.
Each habit prevents a real failure: a leaked key, a frozen agent, a blocked account, or a flooded context.

slides.title: Where does the API key go?

left.label: In the prompt
points: The model can see it, so it can repeat it
It lands in logs and saved traces
A clever customer might coax it out
Anyone with the transcript has your key

right.label: In the environment
points: The model only ever sees the result
Change the key without touching code

sentences: One mistake deserves its own slide: putting an API key where the model can see it.
If the key is in the prompt, the model can repeat it, in a reply or in a log.
Traces and transcripts get shared, and the key travels with them.
And a customer who asks cleverly enough might talk Scout into printing it.
Instead, set the key as an environment variable, just like your Anthropic key in Module 1.
Your track parcel function reads it, and the model only ever sees the tracking result.

slides.title: When ParcelPath says slow down

messages.label: Your code
messages.text: Waits 2 seconds, then tries once more

messages.label: ParcelPath
messages.text: 200 OK · in transit · last scan Denver hub · due Thursday

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: Your tent is on its way and should arrive on Thursday.

aside.label: Busy hours
aside.text: Cache recent lookups for a few minutes, so the same parcel isn't fetched twenty times.

sentences: Busy hours bring a different problem: rate limits.
Scout asks to track Ana's parcel during the lunchtime rush.
ParcelPath answers with status four twenty-nine, too many requests, and says to retry after two seconds.
Your code, not the model, waits the two seconds and tries once more.
This time the call succeeds.
Scout gets a clean result and answers Ana, without ever knowing there was a hiccup.
When many customers ask at once, also cache recent lookups, so the same parcel is not fetched twenty times a minute.

slides.title: Return only what the model needs

cells: Yes, for where is it now
Dozens of scan events, depot codes, barcodes

note.text: About 4,000 lines in, three fields out: fewer tokens, lower cost, fewer mistakes.

sentences: The last habit is trimming the result.
ParcelPath's full answer is huge, but Scout mostly needs two things: the status and the expected delivery day.
The last scan helps too, for customers who ask where exactly the parcel is.
Scout does not need dozens of scan events, depot codes and barcodes.
And some fields, like a driver's notes, should never reach a customer at all.
Trimming takes the result from thousands of lines to three fields, which means fewer tokens, lower cost and fewer mistakes.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: Wrap each API in a thin function and define it as a tool
Keys live in the environment, never in the prompt
Give every call a timeout, and slow down on a 429
Return only the fields the model needs

sentences: Let us pull it together.
Wrap each API in a thin function with a clear name, and define it as a tool.
Keep keys in the environment, where your code can read them and the model cannot.
Give every call a timeout, and slow down when the API answers four twenty-nine.
Return only the fields the model needs.
Next: what to do when a tool fails anyway, because sooner or later, it will.

midQuiz.q: Where should Scout's ParcelPath API key live?
options: In the system prompt, so Scout can use it when it needs to
In an environment variable that your track_parcel code reads
midQuiz.explain: The model never needs the key. Your code reads it from the environment and calls ParcelPath; the model only sees the result.
midQuiz.hint: Who actually calls ParcelPath: the model, or your code?

midQuiz.q: Why does every ParcelPath call get a timeout?
options: So a slow or hung server can't freeze Scout
Because the model will refuse to call tools without one
midQuiz.explain: Without a timeout, a call can wait forever while the customer waits too. A timeout turns a hang into an error your code can handle.
midQuiz.hint: What happens to a waiting customer if ParcelPath never answers?

endQuiz.q: During a busy hour, ParcelPath answers 429. What does that mean?
options: Too many requests: wait, then try again
endQuiz.explain: 429 is a rate limit. Wait as long as the API asks, retry, and cache recent lookups so you send fewer requests.
endQuiz.hint: Think busy hour, not bad input.

endQuiz.q: ParcelPath returns about 4,000 lines of JSON for one parcel. What should track_parcel give Scout?
options: All of it, so Scout has every detail
The status, the expected delivery and the last scan
Nothing; Scout can call ParcelPath itself
endQuiz.explain: Those fields answer the questions customers ask. Fewer tokens means faster, cheaper, more accurate replies, and private fields stay out.
endQuiz.hint: Which fields would answer: where is it, and when will it arrive?
